context.text: Christianity had touched Rus before Vladimir: Patriarch Photius counted the Rus among the peoples receiving a bishop in the 860s, and Vladimir's grandmother, Princess Olga, was baptized at Constantinople around 957. But the land remained pagan, and Vladimir himself began as a fierce pagan prince.

narrative.text: The Primary Chronicle tells how Vladimir examined the faiths of his neighbors, and how his envoys, returning from the Liturgy in Hagia Sophia, reported: 'We knew not whether we were in heaven or on earth, for on earth there is no such splendor or beauty... we only know that God dwells there among men.' Beauty, not argument, decided the matter — a story Orthodoxy has always loved to tell of itself.

The political frame is documented from the Byzantine side as well: around 987–988 Vladimir aided the emperor Basil II against rebellion, received his sister Anna in marriage — an unheard-of concession — was baptized, and took Cherson in the Crimea amid the negotiations. Returning to Kiev, he cast the idol of Perun into the Dnieper and had the people of Kiev baptized in its waters, conventionally in 988. Churches, schools, and a metropolitan see under Constantinople followed.

significance.text: From Vladimir's baptism grows the Orthodoxy of the eastern Slavs — of Kiev, and later Moscow — in time the most populous branch of the Orthodox world, heir of the Slavonic books of Cyril and Methodius's disciples. The Church venerates Vladimir and Olga as equals of the apostles, and 988 as one of history's decisive dates.

uncertainty: The year 988 and the Dnieper baptism follow the Primary Chronicle, compiled over a century later and blending record with legend (the 'testing of the faiths' is a literary set piece); the Byzantine alliance, marriage, and Vladimir's conversion c. 987–989 are historically secure.
